title: Bowing
hook: bowing in all schools, from a small bow to full prostration

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name chanted: Namo Amituofo, said step by step around a Chinese hall. Your line was walking the name. Which walk did you turn into practice? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

Soon after his awakening, an old discourse says, the Buddha sat alone and had a surprising thought. It is hard, he reflected, to live without someone to honor and respect. So he looked around for someone wiser to bow to. In the whole world, he could find no one. So he decided to honor the truth he had awakened to, the Dhamma itself. Even the awakened one, in this story, wanted something to honor. Today: bowing.
screen: `JUST AFTER AWAKENING.` → `SOMEONE TO HONOR.` → `HE HONORS THE DHAMMA.`

segments.voice: First, the small bow. Across Buddhist schools, the simplest bow is palms together at the chest and a slight bend forward. Zen calls the folded hands gassho. It greets a teacher, a friend, a meal, a cushion before sitting on it. Second, the kneeling bow. In Theravada temples in places like Thailand and Sri Lanka, people kneel and lower forehead, forearms and knees to the floor, often three times: once for the Buddha, once for the Dhamma, once for the Sangha. Children learn it young, and adults do it on entering a shrine room, before a monk, or before going to sleep. Third, the full prostration. In Tibetan practice, people stretch the whole body flat on the ground, arms out ahead, then rise and do it again. Some do this as a daily practice in a shrine room; some pilgrims travel long roads this way, one body length at a time. Fourth, what a bow is for. Buddhist teachers say a bow is not groveling, and not worship of a statue. It's a practice of lowering the self, of letting the proudest part of you, the head, touch the same floor as the feet. In Zen, some teachers say that in a true bow there is no one bowing and nothing bowed to. In the Theravada telling, it is honoring what is worth honoring, as the Buddha himself chose to honor the Dhamma. Different schools, different heights, one movement: down, and back up.
screen: `PALMS TOGETHER: THE SMALL BOW.` · `KNEELING: BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `THE WHOLE BODY ON THE GROUND.` · `THE HEAD MEETS THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `DOWN, AND BACK UP.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to try it, if you'd like. Bring your palms together at your chest. Bow three times, as deep as is comfortable for your body: a nod of the head, a bend at the waist, or kneeling and touching the floor. Go slowly. On the way down, notice what lowering feels like. On the way up, notice what rising feels like. If you're a Buddhist, you may bow to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. If not, you can bow to whatever in your life you honor: a teacher, a parent, the day itself. Then sit quietly. The bell holds the time.
Bowing. Lowering the body in respect, from palms together and a slight nod to the whole body flat on the ground. School by school, the form changes. Today's word.
Your line: bow. Today, before one small thing, a meal, a hard conversation, your bed tonight, give a slight bow, even just in your head. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhists bow in their own ways: Zen practitioners bow with palms together, Theravada Buddhists kneel and touch the floor, often three times for the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and Tibetan Buddhists practice full-length prostrations.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, newly awake. it feels hard to live without someone to honor, but you find no one wiser than you. what do you do?
options: decide you need to honor no one.
honor the Dhamma, the truth you awakened to.
go looking for a teacher anyway.
fork.reveal: in the discourse, he chooses to honor and respect the Dhamma itself. even the awakened one honors something.

original.note: Pali vandana: homage, respectful salutation, the bow and the words said with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: bowing is a polite nod, or worship of a statue.
what it means: lowering the self, from palms together to the whole body on the ground, to honor what is worth honoring.
what a scholar hears: the Buddha, newly awake, choosing to honor the Dhamma; vandana; the three bows for Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.

notes: SN 6.2 (Garava Sutta) paraphrased: after awakening, the Buddha reflects that it is painful to dwell without reverence, finds no one superior, and resolves to honor the Dhamma. Confirm paraphrase and placement 'just after his awakening'.
The kneeling bow described (forehead, forearms and knees) without naming the five-point count; 'often three times' for Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha. Confirm.
Thailand and Sri Lanka named as examples of Theravada bowing practice; confirm.
Tibetan full-length prostrations and pilgrims who prostrate along long roads; confirm.
Zen sayings about bowing ('no one bowing and nothing bowed to') attributed to 'some teachers'; confirm acceptable as a paraphrase of a common Zen teaching.

Editor: SN 6.2 says the Buddha resolved to honor and respect the Dhamma, not that he bowed; changed 'bowed to the Dhamma' wording in hook, teach, screen and fork. 'Just after' softened to 'soon after'; 'the old discourses' to 'an old discourse'. Cut 'every school' and 'often say' claims in word, howItsDone and myth.
